title: Auditioning for Sevitzky, the weekly bass lessons and the Flat or Sharp joke
summary: He recounts his Chicago audition, the $35-a-week job, Sevitzky's one-by-one rehearsal tactics and bass lessons, and getting a pink slip after quipping 'Dr. Flat or Sharp'.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Well, I didn't care much for him for the fact that he didn't care much for me. He made it pretty miserable on me when I... All the nine years I worked over there for some reason or other. Of course, he was a strict old country Russian type, you know. And I don't know, it seems to me he had a grudge against something and he was taking it out on people. He made it tough for a lot of good musicians over there. He's teaching at the University of Miami now. Married into big money, you know. As a conductor, he never did make it very much. How's that level doing? Yeah, it's pretty good. Well, anyway, he was a bass player originally. And, I don't know, somehow or other somebody put it in his head that he was a conductor. So he became a conductor. He was married to this Maria Kusevitsky, related to the Serg Kusevitsky, the famous Boston Symphony Orchestra conductor. And, you know, one thing pulled and money and the other. But, before you know it, the guy's got a baton in his hands and he's conducting the Indianapolis Symphony. And, I was at the Musicians' Union in Chicago one day, shooting the bull with all the musicians, you know. Like in New York, in Chicago, all the big towns. When you're not working, all you do is go to the union and stay there all day long. And, there was a letter on the bulletin board that says, young musicians, if you want to audition, there are openings for so many violins, so many violins, so many violins, so many cellos, and so many basses in the Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra. And, auditions will be held for so many of the day. So I picked up my bass today and went up there and I was at one of the swanky hotels in Chicago with a Blackhawk I think it was. Blackstone, Blackstone. And there were quite a few young guys from Chicago and good musicians auditioning. And we noticed that as they came out of the audition, they were all shook up. They were either pale white in the face or shaking or something. So I was thinking, gee, this guy must be real tough, you know. So I went in there and I did my audition. And he asked me, he says, what is your name? And I told him, he says, how old you are? I said, well, I'm 19 years old. You are sure? And he says, well, play something. So I played a little something and then he gave me something to sight read. And he says, all right, that's enough. Sit down. So I sat down and he says, how you would like to play in my orchestra? Just like that. I said, well, I like it fine. He says, all right. He says, it paid $35 a week. 20-week season. But you must practice. If you don't practice, it's too bad, you know. So that was it. And out I go, you know, I kept practicing, all right. And the season opened, came up and I packed my bags and went to Indianapolis. And boy, oh boy, when rehearsals started, it was tough. This guy was, he would make you play one by one, you know, stop the orchestra. Instead of rehearsing what was important, he'd just make everybody play one by one. He's wasting time. So he's making everybody nervous. And before he knew it, we got his number. And naturally, being a bass player, he made it tough on bass players. And, you know, this got to be a drag after a while. Play one by one alone all the time. Gee, he started getting nervous. He got the idea also that he would teach the bass section and give them a lesson every week. So every once a week, we had to go to Jordan Conservatory and line up and have him give us a lesson. Well, I got so, every time it was my turn, he would say, Mazzari, you are flat. Go home and practice. And the next week, it'd be, Mazzari, you are sharp. Go home and practice. And he wouldn't let me play two notes, you know, something like that. So, one fine day, I don't know what hit me, but it was my turn to play. So I said, well, how do you want it today, Dr. Flat or Sharp? And I got a pink slip right there because all the other bass players laughed. By the way, there are testimonies that I originated that joke in case anybody wants to steal it. I'm the originator of it because I have seven other witnesses. I'm familiar with Fabian, but I doubt if he won't testify to it, you know. So I got the pink slip that time. I got a letter from the manager. It says, it is my painful duty to inform you that your services are no longer required. So I went through the whole summer wondering when I was going to get a job next winter, of course. I never worked in the summer, hardly. You know, it's pretty hard for a musician to get jobs in the summer. Meanwhile, the union in Indianapolis met and decided that since I was a local member of the union, that I should have a job. And so when Fabian started to import a bass player from New York, from out of town, they said, uh-uh, Mazzari here is a local guy and I think we should use him. Well, that made Fabian very mad, so he made him play another audition. So I remember by that time he got into this kick about auditioning guys in a dark theater where you couldn't see where he was and you were on the stage all alone with all the lights they could dig up, you know, on you. Isn't that ridiculous?
